title: Sponsored Ingredients for Food Creators: How You Earn
summary: Sponsored ingredients for food creators, explained: how a brand owns one slot in your recipe, how it stacks with grocery commissions, and disclosure.
body_markdown:
Sponsored ingredients for food creators are the quietest brand deal you can take. A brand pays to own one ingredient slot in a recipe you already publish, so its product is the one readers see and add to their cart. You don't shoot a new video or write a new post.


Our view: for most recipe creators, this beats a one-off sponsored post when the recipe already calls for that ingredient, and it's a bad deal when it doesn't. The rest of this post explains how the placement works on the creator side, how it stacks with grocery commissions, and how to tell the two cases apart.


## What is a sponsored ingredient?


A sponsored ingredient is a paid placement where a brand's product becomes the named item in one slot of your recipe's shoppable ingredient list. If your avocado toast lists "1 loaf sourdough bread", a bakery brand can own that line, so readers who shop the recipe get that loaf in their cart.


The recipe stays yours. The method, the photos and the other ingredients don't change. Only one line in the list carries a brand.


## How is a sponsored ingredient different from a sponsored post?


A sponsored post is new content made for a brand. A sponsored ingredient is a placement inside content you've already made. That difference changes the workload, the timeline and the risk.

## How do sponsored ingredients and grocery commissions stack?


They stack because both run on the same shoppable ingredient list. Readers who shop the recipe earn you a grocery commission on what they buy, and the sponsored slot means one of those items is a brand that paid for the spot.


Jupiter describes the two income lines for creators who


[apply to Jupiter](https://www.jupiter.co/apply)


: commission on what readers actually buy, attributed to the exact post, and brand campaigns where you're "paid for the post itself, or for making a brand's product the ingredient in your recipe."


Jupiter doesn't publish a payout split for sponsored ingredients as of October 2026. Ask for the terms of each campaign in writing before you accept it, and check whether the fee is flat or tied to performance.

## How do you keep a sponsored ingredient honest?


Keep it honest by disclosing it every time and only accepting products you'd cook with anyway. US creators fall under the FTC's Endorsement Guides, which say a


[material connection must be disclosed](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-255/section-255.5)


clearly and conspicuously. Payment and free product both count, and the same section covers affiliate links on blogs.


A practical checklist before you accept a slot:


-


You've cooked the recipe with that exact product and it works.


-


The product is sold where your readers shop, or the cart will fail.


-


A plain label such as "Sponsored" sits next to the ingredient itself, with a second one in the footer if you like.


-


Any Reel or story that promotes the recipe also says it includes a paid placement.


-


You'd still publish the recipe the same way if the placement ended tomorrow.


This post doesn't cover what brands pay for a slot. That's a brand-side question, and our sister site explains

## Sponsored ingredients for food creators: who is a good fit?


Creators whose recipes lean on everyday grocery staples are the best fit: bread, pasta, beans, broth, eggs, dairy, oils and sauces. A brand can own one of those lines without changing the dish.


Creators who mainly post restaurant reviews or highly regional cooking with hard-to-find ingredients will see fewer slots, since the product has to be in stock where readers shop.


Follower count matters less than you'd think. Jupiter says there's no follower minimum, and brands look at whether your audience actually cooks. Our guide to
